spatial_entity.notes: Analytical archipelago-level social-history target before full political unification. The claim must not be represented by the later Kingdom of Hawaiʻi as though all islands formed one polity throughout the interval.

claim.date_text_original: late precontact and early contact era, before complete archipelago unification
claim.summary: Indigenous Hawaiian historical traditions and later specialist scholarship describe kauwā as a small, hereditary and strongly segregated status group within late precontact Hawaiian society. Accounts describe endogamy, stigma, separate landholding or residence, subordination to masters, and selection of kauwā for ritual sacrifice. Because Hawaiian uses of kauwā are context-sensitive and the surviving detailed descriptions were recorded in the nineteenth century, the atlas classifies this as institutional other servile dependency at P3 rather than assuming that every occurrence of kauwā is equivalent to chattel slavery.

territorial_practice.notes: P3 reflects a hereditary, socially structured status category, not demographic prevalence. Modern scholarship describes the class as very small. The classification deliberately retains the indigenous term and avoids treating all Hawaiian service relationships or all uses of kauwā as slavery.

source.title: Kepelino's Traditions of Hawaii
source.author_or_institution: Kepelino Keauokalani; edited by Martha Warren Beckwith
source.temporal_scope: Retrospective account of precontact and early nineteenth-century Hawaiian society
source.independence_notes: Indigenous Hawaiian historical tradition written in the nineteenth century and published with Hawaiian text and English translation.
source.reliability_limitations: Retrospective rather than a contemporaneous eighteenth-century observation. Beckwith's English rendering uses 'slave' for kauwā; terminology and social status must therefore be interpreted with other Hawaiian accounts and modern scholarship.

evidence.evidence_role: indigenous account of hereditary kauwā status, segregation, masters, and ritual killing

source.title: Hawaiian Antiquities (Moolelo Hawaii)
source.author_or_institution: David Malo; translated/edited in Bishop Museum edition
source.temporal_scope: Retrospective account of precontact Hawaiian institutions
source.independence_notes: Nineteenth-century Native Hawaiian account of traditional institutions, independent in authorship from Kepelino.
source.reliability_limitations: Retrospective and mediated by translation/editorial history. Malo explicitly notes multiple meanings/usages around kauwā, so the term should not be flattened into one universal English status.

version.version_label: Bernice P. Bishop Museum Special Publication 2, 1951 edition

evidence.evidence_role: indigenous historical account of kauwā and Hawaiian social hierarchy

source.title: The Evolution of Private Property in Nineteenth-Century Hawaii
source.author_or_institution: Sumner J. La Croix and James Roumasset
source.independence_notes: Modern economic-historical synthesis drawing on Hawaiian historical scholarship.
source.reliability_limitations: The article is principally about land/property institutions, not slavery; its description of kauwā is contextual and should not carry the classification alone.

evidence.evidence_role: modern contextual synthesis identifying kauwā as a very small third status class
evidence.locator: note 6: 'a third very small class' identified as kauwā
